new.analysis:
## How the week went
None of the three planned walk-runs happened between Sep 21 and 27, though the rest days held. Your check-in shows good sleep, low stress and a body that feels fine, so this looks like a busy week rather than a warning sign. One week off costs very little fitness at this stage.

## Why the plan restarts where it does
Your last runs were Sep 14 – 20, a gentle return after the cold, and the longest was 24.5 minutes on Sep 19. Monday and Wednesday repeat that level so you can get back into the rhythm gently. Saturday keeps you moving forward, because there are no spare weeks before the race.

## The road to Sun Nov 15
At an easy pace, running 5K without walking will likely take 40 minutes or a bit more. Getting there from 2-minute runs in six weeks is realistic, but only if most weeks go to plan. Here is the rough shape, which will shift depending on how each week goes:

| Week | Longest running stretch |
| --- | --- |
| Sep 28 – Oct 4 | 2 to 3 minutes |
| Oct 5 – 11 | 3 to 5 minutes |
| Oct 12 – 18 | 5 to 8 minutes |
| Oct 19 – 25 | 10 to 15 minutes |
| Oct 26 – Nov 1 | 20 minutes non-stop |
| Nov 2 – 8 | 25 to 30 minutes non-stop |
| Nov 9 – 15 | short easy runs, then race day |

The cold and the missed week already gave your body two quiet weeks, so race week will be your lighter week. If the build slips, we can plan the race with short walk breaks, and that would still be a strong first 5K.

## Why there are no speed sessions
At this stage of training, experienced runners add faster running. For you, building means making the running stretches longer, and that is the whole job. Hard efforts would tire you out and make those stretches harder to extend.

## How hard the running should feel
Your running bits have felt 6 to 7 out of 10, with heart rate averaging 132 to 139 across each session. That is fine for walk-run, but the next steps need the running to feel easier. Slow down until you can speak in short sentences, because nobody is timing the running bits.

## Keeping the three mornings
If a morning falls through, run the next day and push the following run back so there is always a day off between runs. Never double up or add a fourth run to make up for a missed one. Your dog walks are a good base and still count as rest days.
